lessons.title: から / ので

cases.situation: Explaining or apologising for something (why you were late, why you cannot come).
cases.guidance: Reach for ので. It frames the reason as a calm explanation of the situation, which sounds considerate and is safe in polite or formal speech. から puts the weight on your reason itself, which in an apology can read as pushing an excuse.

lessons.title: だから / なぜなら / ことから

cases.situation: Writing an essay or a report, and setting out the reason for the claim you just made.
cases.guidance: Use なぜなら, and close the sentence with からです. It announces that an explanation is coming, which is what written argument wants. だから is the spoken 'so' and reads as blunt on the page; bare から buries the reason inside the sentence instead of presenting it.

cases.situation: Saying what a conclusion was inferred from, rather than why something happened.
cases.guidance: Use ことから. It points at the evidence a judgement rests on ('from the fact that X, we can say Y'), which is why it turns up in explanations of names, origins and findings. なぜなら gives the cause of an event, not the grounds for an inference.

lessons.title: ので / し

cases.situation: You have more than one reason, and you want it heard that there is more than one.
cases.guidance: Use し, repeated on each reason: 安いし、近いし. It signals the list is not exhaustive, so it suits piling up justifications. ので gives one reason and closes the matter, so stacking ので sounds like you keep starting over.

lessons.title: おかげで / ばかりに

cases.situation: Naming the cause of an outcome that was clearly good, or clearly bad.
cases.guidance: Here the outcome decides, not the register. おかげで credits a cause for a welcome result ('thanks to X'). ばかりに blames a cause for an unwelcome one ('simply because of X, and it went wrong'). Using おかげで for a bad result reads as sarcasm.

lessons.title: おかげで / んだもん

cases.situation: Defending yourself after being told off, in casual speech.
cases.guidance: んだもん is the pouty 'but I had to, didn't I' of a child or of someone playing at being one. It states a reason and sulks at the same time, so it lands badly with anyone you owe politeness to. おかげで is neutral and credits a cause; it cannot carry that defensive tone at all.

lessons.title: だって / ものだから

cases.situation: Excusing something unexpected you did, to someone you are not close to.
cases.guidance: Use ものだから. It offers the circumstance as the thing that made you act, which reads as an explanation rather than a protest. だって opens with the protest itself and sounds childish or argumentative to anyone senior to you.

lessons.title: がゆえに / こととて

cases.situation: The cause has to modify a noun rather than lead into a clause.
cases.guidance: Use がゆえの before the noun: 若さがゆえの過ち. がゆえに is the adverbial form and needs a predicate to attach to. Same word, two slots, and picking the wrong one leaves the sentence ungrammatical rather than merely odd.

cases.situation: Apologising in formal writing for something the circumstances made unavoidable.
cases.guidance: Use こととて. It excuses the outcome as forgivable given the situation, which is why it appears in written apologies. がゆえに only asserts the logical cause, with no plea attached, so it sounds like an explanation for why you are not sorry.

lessons.title: でも / けど / しかし

cases.situation: Writing an essay, a news article, or giving a formal presentation.
cases.guidance: Use しかし. けど and でも are the everyday spoken 'but' and read as too casual in writing. しかし is the neutral written contrast; だが is a blunter written alternative, and けれども is more formal still.

lessons.title: でも / それでも

cases.situation: The second statement holds true even though the first would lead you to expect otherwise.
cases.guidance: Use それでも ('even so', 'nevertheless') when you concede the first point and assert the second anyway. Plain でも only marks a contrast; それでも adds that the result defies what the first clause implies.

lessons.title: ただ / ただし / もっとも

cases.situation: Stating a rule or an offer, then attaching the condition it comes with.
cases.guidance: Use ただし. It introduces a binding exception to what was just stated, which is why it runs through contracts, notices and terms. ただ softens with a passing reservation ('though, mind you') and is too loose to carry a condition anyone has to obey.

cases.situation: You want to take some of the force out of a claim you have just made yourself.
cases.guidance: Use もっとも. It concedes a qualification to your own statement ('though, to be fair...'), so the sentence reads as a considered position. ただ just adds a separate reservation and does not carry that self-correcting tone.

lessons.title: なきゃ / なければならない

cases.situation: Writing, or speaking in a formal setting (a report, an announcement, talking to a superior).
cases.guidance: Use なければならない, the full uncontracted form. なきゃいけない and なくちゃいけない are casual spoken contractions that sound too informal in writing. ねばならない is a step more literary again, common in rules and textbooks.

lessons.title: 帰る / 戻る

cases.situation: Saying you will go back somewhere: is it the place you belong, or a spot you had left and are now reversing to?
cases.guidance: Reach for 戻る when you are reversing to a place or state you had left: back to your desk, back to the previous page, back to how things were. 帰る is for returning to a place you belong (home, your hometown, your country), so 家に戻る makes home sound like a spot you are retracing to rather than where you actually belong.

lessons.title: あとで / てから

cases.situation: Saying you will do the second thing only once the first is finished.
cases.guidance: Use てから. It attaches to a verb and insists on the order: 手を洗ってから食べる means the washing comes first. あとで attaches to a noun (食事のあとで) and only places one event later than another, without that 'not until' force.

lessons.title: あげく / 上で / 末

cases.situation: The second action was decided on the basis of the first, not merely after it.
cases.guidance: Use 上で. It says the first step supplied the grounds for the second: 相談した上で決める. あげく also means 'after all that', but it carries the outcome being a bad one, so it makes a neutral decision sound like a debacle.

cases.situation: After a long, effortful process, something finally resolved.
cases.guidance: Use 末. It foregrounds the length and the effort, and the outcome may be good or bad. あげく shares the 'after a drawn-out business' framing but always lands on an unwelcome result, so it cannot report a hard-won success.

cases.situation: Marking a point in time since which a condition has held.
cases.guidance: Use 以来 for a lasting change dating from that point: 卒業以来会っていない. たきり fixes on a single event that was never followed up (出かけたきり帰らない), so it needs that one-off action, not a general starting line.

lessons.title: ごろ / くらい

cases.situation: Saying 'about' a number: is it a point in time, or an amount, degree, or duration?
cases.guidance: Use くらい (or ぐらい) for approximate amounts, degrees and durations: 一時間くらい, これくらい, 千円くらい. Reach for ごろ only for an approximate point in time: 三時ごろ, 来週ごろ. ごろ can never mark a quantity, so 一時間ごろ is wrong.

cases.situation: Choosing between くらい and ぐらい for the same approximate amount.
cases.guidance: Nothing rides on this one. ぐらい is the slightly more colloquial voicing of the same word and both are accepted everywhere; pick either and stay consistent within a sentence.

lessons.title: や〜など / たり〜たり

cases.situation: Giving a few representative examples: are they things, or things you did?
cases.guidance: Use たり〜たり for actions (読んだり書いたりした), and や〜など for nouns (本やノートなど). Both mean the list is partial, but たり conjugates the verbs, so it is the only one that can list what happened rather than what was there.

cases.situation: You want the 'and so on' without pairing it with や.
cases.guidance: など stands on its own after a single noun (コーヒーなど), which や cannot do: や needs two items to sit between. Used alone after one item, など also works as a softener, offering it as a suggestion rather than the only option.

lessons.title: そして / それから

cases.situation: Joining two actions: just 'and', or 'and then' with the second clearly following the first?
cases.guidance: Use それから when the second action comes after the first in time: 朝ごはんを食べて、それから学校へ行きます. そして simply links two things ('and') without stressing order, so it also fits listing traits or simultaneous facts where それから would imply a wrong sequence.

lessons.title: その上 / おまけに / しかも / なお

cases.situation: Adding a second fact that makes the first more striking than it already was.
cases.guidance: Use しかも. It piles on in a way that says 'and on top of that, of all things', which works in speech and in writing. おまけに is casual and carries a grumbling or gleeful tone, so it flattens a serious point into an anecdote.

cases.situation: Appending a note to an official announcement or a written notice.
cases.guidance: Use なお. It introduces supplementary information in documents ('note that...'), which is the one job the others cannot do. その上 adds weight to the preceding point conversationally and reads as out of place in a formal notice.

lessons.title: ましょう / ませんか / いかがですか

cases.situation: Suggesting something to someone who may well not want to.
cases.guidance: Use ませんか. Phrasing the invitation as a negative question leaves them room to decline, which is why it is the polite default. ましょう assumes agreement and works best once the plan is already settled, or with people you are close to.

cases.situation: Offering something rather than proposing to do something together.
cases.guidance: Use いかがですか. It asks after their preference about a thing (コーヒーはいかがですか), so it fits offers and hospitality. ませんか proposes a joint action and needs a verb, so it cannot offer an object at all.

lessons.title: あげます / くれます

cases.situation: Someone gives something to you (or to your family, your team, your side).
cases.guidance: Use くれる. Japanese picks the giving verb by direction, not by politeness: あげる always points away from the speaker, くれる always points towards. 友達に本をあげた is you giving; 友達が本をくれた is them giving to you, and swapping them reverses who did what.

lessons.title: くださる / さしあげる

cases.situation: Someone senior to you gave you something.
cases.guidance: Use くださる. Direction is still inward, same as くれる, but くださる raises the giver, which is what you want for a teacher, a client or a boss. Plain くれる for a superior is not rude so much as flat, and in a thank-you it reads as careless.

cases.situation: You are giving something to someone senior to you.
cases.guidance: Use さしあげる, the humble outward form, which lowers you rather than raising them. Be sparing with it: said to the person's face it can sound as if you are drawing attention to the favour, so plain あげます is often the safer choice in the moment.

lessons.title: に もらいます / から もらいます

cases.situation: Naming who or what you received from, when the giver is an organisation rather than a person.
cases.guidance: Use から. に and から are both fine for a person (友達にもらった / 友達からもらった), but only から works for a company, a school or an office, where に would read as marking a destination instead of a source.

lessons.title: もらう / いただく

cases.situation: Saying you received something from someone senior to you.
cases.guidance: Use いただく. It is the humble counterpart of もらう and lowers you relative to the giver, which is what politeness needs here. The direction is identical; only your position in it changes.

benefactive-action.name: Benefactive Action (Doing X As A Favor)

lessons.title: てあげる / てくれる / てもらう

cases.situation: Someone did something for you, and you are deciding which of you is the subject of the sentence.
cases.guidance: Both describe the same favour. てくれる makes the doer the subject (友達が手伝ってくれた), and てもらう makes you the subject (友達に手伝ってもらった). てもらう also implies you asked; てくれる leaves it as something they did of their own accord, which is why it sounds warmer.

cases.situation: You want to offer to do something for someone senior to you.
cases.guidance: てさしあげる is the humble form, but it is risky: announcing your own favour draws attention to it whichever form you use. In practice offer with ましょうか instead, and keep てあげる for equals and てさしあげる for describing the act afterwards.

lessons.title: てくれませんか / ていただけませんか

cases.situation: Asking a favour of a client, or of someone you have no standing to ask.
cases.guidance: Use ていただけませんか. The humble verb plus the negative potential question makes the request as tentative as Japanese gets, which is what a large or awkward ask needs. てくれませんか is the everyday version and sounds under-dressed for it.

cases.situation: Leaving the decision genuinely with them, rather than stating what you want.
cases.guidance: ていただけませんか asks whether they are able to, so the answer is theirs. ていただきたい states your wish and puts the weight on you: polite, but firmer, and it suits instructions from a position of authority more than it suits a favour.

lessons.title: てはいけない / てはならない / べきではない

cases.situation: Writing a rule, a warning notice, or a legal provision.
cases.guidance: Use てはならない. It is the formal, written prohibition and carries the weight of a rule that stands independently of who is speaking. てはいけない is the everyday one, used to children and in day-to-day instructions, and looks slight on a sign.

cases.situation: Saying something is wrong to do, without claiming it is forbidden.
cases.guidance: Use べきではない. It is a judgement about what is proper, so it fits opinion and argument. てはならない states a prohibition that someone has the authority to impose, which is a claim you often cannot actually make.

lessons.title: たらいい / たらいかがですか

cases.situation: Suggesting a course of action to a customer, a guest, or someone senior.
cases.guidance: Use たらいかがですか. It is the polite suggestion form and keeps the decision visibly theirs. たらいい, といい and ばいい are all casual and near-interchangeable with each other, but any of them to a superior reads as telling them what to do.

lessons.title: ことだ / はずだ

cases.situation: Saying something 'should' be so: is it advice, or a prediction?
cases.guidance: はずだ is expectation from reasoning ('it should be true, given what I know'), and says nothing about what anyone ought to do. ことだ is direct advice ('what you should do is...'). English 'should' covers both, which is exactly why they get swapped.

lessons.title: つもり / ようと思う

cases.situation: Mentioning a plan you have not fully committed to.
cases.guidance: Use ようと思う. It presents the intention as a current thought, so it leaves room to change your mind and sounds less presumptuous when the plan involves other people. つもり states a settled intention and can come across as a decision already taken.

lessons.title: つもりだ / つもりで

cases.situation: The intention has to lead into another clause rather than end the sentence.
cases.guidance: Use つもりで: 一日で終わらせるつもりで始めた. つもりだ closes a sentence and cannot be followed by a main clause. Same meaning, different slot, and the wrong one simply will not attach.

lessons.title: ために / ように

cases.situation: The aim is something you cannot simply decide to do: hearing better, not forgetting, a door not closing.
cases.guidance: Use ように. It pairs with potential forms, negatives and verbs describing states, because the goal is a condition you hope holds. ために needs a deliberate act with the same subject, so 聞こえるために is wrong where 聞こえるように is right.

lessons.title: べく / んがために

cases.situation: Writing about a purpose pursued with unusual determination.
cases.guidance: んがために is the more emphatic and more archaic of the two, and it colours the purpose as single-minded, sometimes to a fault. べく is the neutral literary 'in order to' and is far commoner in ordinary formal prose.

lessons.title: かもしれない / だろう / ようだ

cases.situation: How sure you are: a bare possibility, or what you actually expect?
cases.guidance: だろう is your expectation ('probably'), so it leans towards the thing being true. かもしれない only concedes that it might be, and works equally for a one-in-ten chance. Using かもしれない where you mean だろう makes you sound noncommittal.

cases.situation: You are basing the guess on something you can see or feel right now.
cases.guidance: Use ようだ. It reports an inference from evidence in front of you (雨が降ったようだ, looking at the wet road). だろう is a judgement from general knowledge and does not claim any particular evidence, so it sounds oddly detached when you are looking straight at it.

cases.situation: Passing on something you were told, in casual conversation.
cases.guidance: Use んだって. It is spoken hearsay and marks the information as second-hand and not yours to vouch for. ようだ claims your own inference from evidence, so using it for something you merely heard overstates what you know.

lessons.title: らしい / ということだ

cases.situation: Relaying information without committing to how reliable it is.
cases.guidance: らしい is loose hearsay: you picked it up somewhere and are not standing behind it. ということだ frames the same content as a definite report from a source, which is why it suits news and official relay. らしい in a report sounds like gossip.

cases.situation: Raising a possibility you think the other person has not considered.
cases.guidance: Use もしかすると〜かもしれない. The もしかすると flags that what follows is a deliberate 'what if', which is what makes it land as a suggestion. ということだ relays a report you received and cannot introduce a hypothesis at all.

lessons.title: とのことだ / とみえて

cases.situation: Formal writing: did you hear it, or are you inferring it from what you observe?
cases.guidance: とみえて draws a conclusion from evidence ('apparently, judging by...') and leads into the clause that follows. とのことだ relays what you were told and closes the sentence. The register is the same; what differs is whether you are citing a source or reading the signs.

lessons.title: みたいだ / かのようだ

cases.situation: Writing a deliberate comparison, where the likeness is the point.
cases.guidance: Use かのようだ. It presents the resemblance as a considered figure of speech, which is why it belongs in description and narrative. みたいだ is the casual spoken 'like', and in writing it reads as an off-hand approximation rather than an image.

lessons.title: かしら / かなあ

cases.situation: Musing out loud in ordinary casual speech.
cases.guidance: かなあ is the safe default for anyone: unisex, current, and neutral in tone. かしら carries a traditionally feminine and somewhat old-fashioned colouring, so it marks the speaker rather than just the musing.

lessons.title: のです / んです

cases.situation: Explaining yourself in ordinary conversation.
cases.guidance: んです is the spoken contraction and is what you will actually hear; のです is the written and formal-speech form. The meaning is identical, so the choice is only about the channel: のです in a report, んです out loud.

lessons.title: たときに / るときに

cases.situation: Where the action of the とき clause sits relative to the main clause.
cases.guidance: This is tense inside the clause, not register. るとき means the action has not yet completed at that moment (日本へ行くときに切符を買う: bought before going), and たとき means it has (日本へ行ったときに買う: bought after arriving). The main verb's tense has no say in it.

lessons.title: の間に / ている間に

cases.situation: The window is defined by something going on, not by a named period.
cases.guidance: Use ている間に: 寝ている間に. の間に needs a noun for the period (休みの間に). Same 間に, and the only question is whether what bounds the window is a stretch of time or an ongoing action.

lessons.title: 中 / ているところ

cases.situation: Saying you are in the middle of doing something, right now.
cases.guidance: Use ているところ. It marks the current stage of an action and is what you reach for when someone interrupts you. 中 attaches to a noun (会議中, 食事中) and labels a state, so it cannot take a verb phrase.

lessons.title: ながら / つつ

cases.situation: Writing, and especially where the two actions sit awkwardly together.
cases.guidance: つつ is the literary ながら, and it has a second use ながら shares only weakly: with a verb of knowing or thinking it becomes concessive (悪いと知りつつ, 'even though I knew'). In ordinary speech about two simultaneous actions, ながら is still the natural one.

lessons.title: しか〜ない / ばかり

cases.situation: 'Only': is it a shortfall, or someone doing the same thing over and over?
cases.guidance: ばかり is about repetition or excess and often carries a complaint (ゲームばかりしている). しか〜ない states a bare restriction with a negative verb (千円しかない) and implies the amount is less than you wanted. They are not interchangeable: ばかり cannot count, and しか cannot grumble.

lessons.title: しかない / だけしか

cases.situation: Stressing how little there is, rather than that you have no choice.
cases.guidance: だけしか doubles up だけ and しか purely for emphasis on the restriction. しかない after a verb is a different thing altogether: 'there is nothing for it but to', a lack of options rather than a lack of quantity.

lessons.title: に過ぎない / に限り / にほかならない

cases.situation: Sizing up a claim: is it merely this, or is it exactly this?
cases.guidance: These point in opposite directions. に過ぎない dismisses ('nothing more than a rumour'), while にほかならない insists ('it is nothing other than proof'). Both translate as 'nothing but', which is why they get swapped, and swapping them inverts your argument.

cases.situation: Writing the terms of an offer or a rule.
cases.guidance: Use に限り. It restricts who or when something applies to (本日に限り半額), which is administrative language, not evaluation. に過ぎない judges something as insignificant and has no place in terms and conditions.

lessons.title: としたら / ものとして

cases.situation: Setting up a working assumption in a written argument or a plan.
cases.guidance: Use ものとして. It fixes a premise that the rest of the reasoning proceeds on, which is why it appears in contracts and planning documents. としたら floats a hypothetical for consideration, so it does not commit the argument to anything.

lessons.title: によれば / に基づいて / を前提として

cases.situation: Naming what a decision or a document was built on, not who said it.
cases.guidance: Use に基づいて. It says the thing was constructed in accordance with a rule, a principle or data. によれば cites a source for a piece of information ('according to the paper') and cannot describe how something was made.

cases.situation: The basis is an assumption being taken as given, not an established rule.
cases.guidance: Use を前提として. It marks something granted for the sake of what follows, which may yet turn out false. に基づいて treats its basis as solid ground, so it quietly asserts more than you may mean.

cases.situation: に即した or に即して: which one attaches where?
cases.guidance: に即した modifies a following noun (実情に即した対応), に即して leads into a verb (実情に即して考える). One word, two slots; the meaning does not change, but the wrong form will not attach.

lessons.title: に先立ち / に先駆けて

cases.situation: Doing something ahead of everyone else, rather than simply beforehand.
cases.guidance: に先駆けて carries being first, ahead of others (世界に先駆けて発売). に先立ち is plain precedence in time, the formal 'prior to' of announcements and ceremonies, with no claim to having beaten anyone to it.

lessons.title: として / を〜として

cases.situation: Someone or something is being treated as a role by another party.
cases.guidance: Use を〜として when there is an object being cast in the role (彼を代表として送る). Bare として says what the subject already is (医者として働く). The を is what shifts it from a description to an act of designation.

lessons.title: に対して / にひきかえ

cases.situation: Setting two things side by side to point out how badly one compares.
cases.guidance: にひきかえ is a pointed, evaluative contrast, usually unflattering to one side. に対して is neutral: it marks a target (質問に対して答える) or a plain contrast between two facts, and carries no verdict.

lessons.title: でしょうがない / 極まりない

cases.situation: Condemning something in writing as beyond acceptable.
cases.guidance: Use 極まりない. It attaches to an evaluative adjective (失礼極まりない) and delivers a judgement, almost always a negative one. でしょうがない reports your own overwhelming feeling in casual speech and cannot pass that kind of verdict.

cases.situation: Grading a quality as extreme, rather than exclaiming about it.
cases.guidance: 極まりない delivers a cold assessment and attaches to an evaluative adjective. といったらありはしない is a dramatic outburst ('you have no idea how...'), so it reports the speaker's state rather than passing judgement on the thing.

lessons.title: にて / をもって / を限りに

cases.situation: Naming the means, or the effective date, in an official announcement.
cases.guidance: Use をもって: 本日をもって終了, 書面をもって通知する. にて marks where something takes place, a stiff old-fashioned で. Both are ceremonial, but only をもって can carry a means or an effective moment.

cases.situation: Announcing that something ends at a given point.
cases.guidance: を限りに specifically marks a cut-off: after this, no more (今年を限りに引退する). をもって can mark the same date neutrally, so it is the one to use when the point is when something takes effect rather than when it stops.

lessons.title: ことはない / までもない / にはあたらない

cases.situation: Formal writing: saying something is too obvious to need stating.
cases.guidance: Use までもない. It says the action would be superfluous (言うまでもなく, 'needless to say'). ことはない is the everyday 'there's no need to' and is usually reassurance offered to a person, which is a different job in a different register.

cases.situation: Saying a step is redundant, rather than that a reaction is unwarranted.
cases.guidance: までもない says the action would be superfluous. にはあたらない says the feeling is not called for (驚くにはあたらない, 'no cause for surprise'). One is about whether a step is necessary, the other about whether a reaction is justified.

occasion.name: Occasion (While Doing / On The Occasion Of)

lessons.title: 際に / にあたり / に際して

cases.situation: Referring to an occasion in ordinary formal writing: a manual, a procedure, an email.
cases.guidance: Use 際に. It is the neutral marker for 'when X happens' and carries no ceremony. にあたり marks the threshold of an undertaking (開会にあたり一言), which is what you want at a podium and far too grand for an instruction.

cases.situation: Referring to a future occasion when you might meet again.
cases.guidance: 折には is the softer, more personal of the two and suits set courtesies (お近くにお越しの折には). に際して is institutional, attached to events and procedures, so it sounds cold in a pleasantry.

lessons.title: かたがた / がてら

cases.situation: Doing a second thing while you are out doing the first.
cases.guidance: がてら is the more everyday of the two and takes concrete errands (散歩がてら買い物). かたがた is stiffer and takes formal purposes, especially courtesies (ご挨拶かたがた伺います), so it is what you write in a letter rather than what you say about a walk.

lessons.title: つまり / すなわち

cases.situation: Restating a term precisely in legal, academic or technical writing.
cases.guidance: Use すなわち. It asserts strict equivalence between the two expressions, which is why definitions use it. つまり summarises loosely ('so, basically'), and in a definition that looseness is exactly what you do not want.

lessons.title: をはじめ / を皮切りに

cases.situation: The first item kicked off a series that kept going.
cases.guidance: Use を皮切りに. It marks a starting point that a sequence unfolded from (東京を皮切りに全国ツアー). をはじめ picks out the most prominent member of a set ('X and others'), with no sequence implied at all.

cases.situation: The phrase has to modify a following noun.
cases.guidance: Use をはじめとする: 日本をはじめとする国々. をはじめとして leads into a clause instead. Same meaning, and the choice is purely about whether a noun or a predicate comes next.

lessons.title: により / にわたって / を通じて

cases.situation: Covering a span: a stretch of time, or an extent of territory.
cases.guidance: Use にわたって for the span itself (三日にわたって, 全国にわたって). により names a means or a cause and cannot measure an extent, so the two only look alike in the English 'through'.

cases.situation: Something passed through stages on the way to where it ended up.
cases.guidance: Use を経て. It traces a path through intermediate steps (交渉を経て合意に至った). を通じて is a channel or a continuous period something happens by or across, without that sense of stages completed one after another.

lessons.title: くせに / ところが / わりには

cases.situation: Telling a story where the outcome was not what anyone expected.
cases.guidance: Use ところが. It is narrative surprise and passes no judgement on anybody. くせに carries open contempt for the subject (知っているくせに教えない), so it turns a plot twist into an accusation.

cases.situation: Something is more, or less, than its circumstances would lead you to expect.
cases.guidance: Use わりには. It measures the outcome against a standard the first clause sets (安いわりにはおいしい). といっても does something else: it walks back an overstatement you just made ('though when I say X, I only mean...').

lessons.title: それなのに / にもかかわらず / に反して

cases.situation: Formal writing, reporting an outcome that ran against the conditions.
cases.guidance: Use にもかかわらず. It is neutral and carries no feeling about the mismatch. それなのに is spoken and openly aggrieved, so it reads as the writer complaining rather than reporting.

cases.situation: The outcome contradicted a specific prediction, expectation or policy.
cases.guidance: Use に反して. It needs something to run counter to: 予想に反して, 意図に反して. にもかかわらず only says the outcome held in spite of a circumstance, without naming anything it contradicted.

lessons.title: といえども / とはいえ / ながらも

cases.situation: Conceding a point you just made, then qualifying it.
cases.guidance: とはいえ is the workable formal one: it accepts what was said and adds the caveat ('that said'). といえども is classical and emphatic ('even X, of all things'), so it overstates an ordinary qualification.

cases.situation: Someone acted against the state they were in.
cases.guidance: Use ながらも. It pairs a state with a contrasting action taken anyway (狭いながらも楽しい我が家), so it attaches inside the clause. とはいえ joins two sentences and cannot bind a state to an action that way.

lessons.title: もし〜たなら / もしも〜なら

cases.situation: The hypothetical is a remote one you want marked as remote.
cases.guidance: もしも is もし with extra weight, so it suits the unlikely and the dramatic (もしもの時, 'if the worst happens'). For an ordinary supposition もし is enough, and もしも can sound theatrical.

lessons.title: すると / からには / 上は

cases.situation: Now that something is settled, saying what you are therefore obliged to do.
cases.guidance: Use からには. It takes a fact as given and draws a resolve or a duty from it (引き受けたからには最後まで). すると simply reports what followed next and carries no obligation at all.

cases.situation: The same 'now that' in formal writing.
cases.guidance: 上は is the written counterpart of からには, near-identical in meaning and stiffer in tone. Use it in documents and formal statements; からには is the one that works out loud.

lessons.title: ともなれば / とあれば / とすると

cases.situation: If the situation calls for it, something will be done regardless of cost.
cases.guidance: Use とあれば. It marks a condition under which the speaker will act anyway (必要とあれば). ともなれば describes what naturally comes with reaching a certain status or scale, which is a statement about the world rather than a commitment.

cases.situation: Reasoning out what would follow from a supposition.
cases.guidance: Use とすると. It is speculative: grant this, and what follows? とあれば assumes the condition will actually obtain and moves to action, so it cannot host a piece of hypothetical reasoning.

lessons.title: たとえ〜ても / どんなに〜ても / にしても

cases.situation: It is the degree that will not change the outcome, not the possibility.
cases.guidance: Use どんなに〜ても: however much, however hard. たとえ〜ても grants that something might happen at all, which is a weaker claim, so it undersells a sentence about no amount of effort being enough.

cases.situation: Granting someone's point in conversation before pushing back.
cases.guidance: にしても is the conversational 'even granting that', and it can pick up something already said (忙しいにしても連絡ぐらいは). たとえ〜ても sets up a hypothetical from scratch and is heavier than a quick concession needs.

lessons.title: ないまでも / としたところで

cases.situation: Granting a supposition and denying that it would change anything.
cases.guidance: Use としたところで. It concedes the case and then dismisses its force ('even supposing so, it makes no difference'). ないまでも does the opposite: it falls short of a maximum but keeps a positive claim ('not quite X, but at least Y').

lessons.title: かわりに / にかわって

cases.situation: Standing in for a person, formally.
cases.guidance: Use にかわって: 社長にかわって挨拶する. It substitutes one party for another and takes a noun. かわりに is broader and can follow a verb phrase ('instead of doing X'), which にかわって cannot do.

lessons.title: すこしも〜ない / 決して〜ない

cases.situation: Making a commitment or a categorical denial.
cases.guidance: Use 決して〜ない. It is a declaration about all occasions ('never, under any circumstances') and belongs to writing and formal speech. すこしも〜ない measures a quantity down to zero ('not in the slightest') and cannot promise anything about the future.

lessons.title: ついでに / ところで

cases.situation: Changing the subject in conversation.
cases.guidance: Use ところで. It is the plain topic-change marker and needs no connection to what came before. ついでに is not a topic shift at all: it adds a second errand onto the first ('while I'm at it'), so it needs an action to piggyback on.

lessons.title: さて / そういえば / ちなみに

cases.situation: Something just said reminded you of a related topic.
cases.guidance: Use そういえば. It marks the new topic as prompted by what was said, which is why it sounds natural and unforced. さて is a deliberate move to the next item, the connective of agendas and speeches, and it ignores whatever triggered the thought.

cases.situation: Adding a side note that supplements the topic rather than replacing it.
cases.guidance: Use ちなみに. It appends related information and stays on topic, which is why it works in writing too. それはそうと drops the current topic to raise a different one, so it reads as an interruption.

lessons.title: 以上 / 限り

cases.situation: A condition that holds for now and may stop holding.
cases.guidance: Use 限り: 体力が続く限り. It tracks a condition while it lasts. 以上 takes a fact as settled and draws a consequent obligation from it ('given that you have accepted, you must'), which is closer to からには than to a running condition.

lessons.title: か〜ないかのうちに / 次第

cases.situation: Promising to do something the moment a condition is met.
cases.guidance: Use 次第: 決まり次第ご連絡します. It attaches to a ます-stem and points forward to something you will do, so it fits business commitments. か〜ないかのうちに narrates two events almost overlapping and cannot carry a promise.

cases.situation: The second thing happened so fast it caught you out.
cases.guidance: Use たかと思ったら. It carries the speaker's surprise at the reversal (泣いたかと思ったら笑っている). か〜ないかのうちに reports the tight timing neutrally, with no reaction attached.

lessons.title: なり / や否や / たが最後

cases.situation: Literary narration: one action followed instantly on another.
cases.guidance: Use なり. It reports immediate succession in written narrative (帰るなり寝てしまった). たが最後 is not about speed: it says that once the first thing happens there is no undoing it, and the consequence is usually bad.

cases.situation: Choosing between the two literary 'no sooner than' forms.
cases.guidance: や否や and なり are close enough that either will pass in most written narration. や否や is the stiffer and more bookish of the two; なり is slightly freer, and is the one that also turns up in older colloquial writing.

lessons.title: ずにはいられない / ていられない / でならない

cases.situation: The situation will not let you carry on as you were.
cases.guidance: Use ていられない: 黙っていられない, 寝てなどいられない. It says continuing is no longer an option given the circumstances. ずにはいられない is an urge you cannot suppress, which is about your own impulse rather than what the situation permits.

cases.situation: An emotion, rather than a physical sensation, that will not let up.
cases.guidance: でならない takes feelings and thoughts (残念でならない, 心配でならない). でたまらない covers intense sensations too (暑くてたまらない), so it is the broader of the two; でならない used of heat or pain sounds wrong.

lessons.title: ずにはすまない / てやまない

cases.situation: Expressing a feeling you have never stopped holding, in formal writing.
cases.guidance: Use てやまない, with the narrow set of verbs it takes (願ってやまない, 期待してやまない). ずにはすまない is an obligation, not a feeling: it says the matter cannot be closed without you doing something, usually apologising or paying.

lessons.title: に応じて / 次第で / 次第です

cases.situation: The outcome is not yet decided and hinges on one factor.
cases.guidance: Use 次第で: 天気次第で中止. It makes the factor decisive for something still open. に応じて describes adjusting in proportion to a factor (収入に応じて), which is a response, not a verdict waiting to be reached.

cases.situation: Closing a formal explanation by saying what the matter rests on.
cases.guidance: 次第です is the polite sentence-final form used to round off an explanation. 次第で sits mid-sentence with the outcome following it. Same word, and the choice is only whether the sentence ends there.

lessons.title: てまで / まで〜て

cases.situation: Where まで sits relative to the verb.
cases.guidance: てまで marks an extreme someone went to in order to achieve something (借金してまで買う), usually with disapproval. The まで〜て ordering is a plain limit instead ('up until X happens'), so the disapproval is not carried over.

lessons.title: ですら / たりとも / にもまして

cases.situation: Citing a striking example to make a general point.
cases.guidance: Use ですら: 専門家ですら間違える. It picks an example so unlikely that it proves the rule. たりとも is absolute negation of even the smallest quantity (一日たりとも忘れない) and needs a negative verb, so it cannot host a positive example.

cases.situation: The 'even' has to land on a に-marked element.
cases.guidance: Use にすら where the noun would take に (子供にすら分かる). ですら fills the subject or topic slot. Same emphasis, different case marking, and the wrong one leaves the particle missing.

cases.situation: Saying something exceeds a benchmark that was already high.
cases.guidance: Use にもまして: 去年にもまして忙しい. It is comparative, so it needs a standard to beat. ですら only nominates a surprising example and makes no comparison of degree at all.

lessons.title: ざるを得ない / よりほかない

cases.situation: Naming the one option that remains.
cases.guidance: よりほかない points at the surviving choice ('there is nothing for it but X'). ざるを得ない says you cannot avoid doing it, framing the same situation as compulsion rather than as a last option. The reluctance is in both; only the framing moves.

lessons.title: ざるを得ない / ずにはおかない / ないではすまない

cases.situation: Something will inevitably produce an effect, whoever is involved.
cases.guidance: Use ずにはおかない. It predicts an unavoidable consequence in the world (見る者を感動させずにはおかない). ざるを得ない is about a person having no choice but to act, so it needs an agent under compulsion.

cases.situation: Social or moral pressure means the matter cannot simply be dropped.
cases.guidance: Use ないではすまない: 謝らないではすまない. The compulsion is other people's expectations, not circumstance. ざるを得ない points at circumstances that leave no alternative and carries no sense of a duty owed.

cases.situation: Circumstances leave you no alternative but to act.
cases.guidance: Use ざるを得ない. It reports an action forced on you by the situation. を禁じ得ない takes an emotion noun (驚きを禁じ得ない) and describes a reaction you could not suppress, so it cannot carry an action at all.

lessons.title: のみならず / ばかりか

cases.situation: The second item is more than you would have expected, not just additional.
cases.guidance: Use ばかりか. It escalates ('not only X but even Y'), and the surprise is the point. のみならず is a neutral formal addition, so it flattens the escalation into a list.

lessons.title: にとどまらず / もさることながら

cases.situation: Both items matter, and the second matters more.
cases.guidance: Use もさることながら. It grants the first its due and then puts the weight on the second (味もさることながら値段が). にとどまらず only says the scope did not stop at the first, without ranking them.

cases.situation: What does not stop at the first item is an action rather than a noun.
cases.guidance: Use the verb-attaching form, Verbる にとどまらず. The noun form takes a noun. Same expression, two attachment points, and the choice is settled by what precedes it.

lessons.title: から見ると / から言うと / の上では

cases.situation: Judging by a criterion, rather than looking from someone's position.
cases.guidance: から言うと introduces the basis you are judging on (経験から言うと). から見ると takes a vantage point, usually a person's or a group's, and reports how things look from there. Both are natural; what changes is whether the noun is a standard or a standpoint.

cases.situation: On paper the figures say one thing, whatever the reality is.
cases.guidance: Use の上では: 計算の上では足りる. It restricts the claim to a formal or technical criterion, often hinting that reality differs. にしたら reports how a situation feels to a particular party and cannot make that on-paper reservation.

lessons.title: につれて / にともなって

cases.situation: One change brought another along with it.
cases.guidance: にともなって allows a one-off event as the trigger (法改正にともなって) and is the more formal of the two. につれて needs both sides to be gradual and continuous, so a single discrete change sits badly with it.

lessons.title: につき / をめぐる / に関わって

cases.situation: The topic is something being argued or fought over.
cases.guidance: Use をめぐる. It implies a contest around the topic (遺産をめぐる争い), which is why it turns up with disputes and debates. につき is the flat administrative 'regarding' or 'per' of notices, with no conflict implied.

cases.situation: Stating a connection to a matter, without claiming any dispute.
cases.guidance: に関わって marks involvement in or connection with something. をめぐる specifically frames the topic as contested, so using it for a plain association overstates the case.

lessons.title: あるいは / にしろ〜にしろ

cases.situation: It does not matter which of the two it turns out to be.
cases.guidance: Use にしろ〜にしろ. The paired form says the outcome is the same either way. あるいは is a plain 'or' offering a choice between alternatives, so it leaves the question open instead of dismissing it.

lessons.title: にかかわらず / を問わず

cases.situation: Writing eligibility terms: an advert, a job posting, an application form.
cases.guidance: Use を問わず: 経験を問わず, 年齢を問わず. It is the set phrase of official notices and takes a bare noun. にかかわらず is the everyday version and takes a wider range of forms, including clauses.

lessons.title: かねない / 恐れがある

cases.situation: A written warning: a forecast, a public notice, a safety advisory.
cases.guidance: Use 恐れがある. It takes a noun or a plain clause and states a risk impersonally, which is what notices need. かねない attaches to a ます-stem and sounds like the speaker's own misgiving, closer to 'could well end up' than to a formal warning.

lessons.title: したがって / そこで

cases.situation: Narrating what you did about a situation.
cases.guidance: Use そこで. It marks the step someone took in response ('so, at that point, I...'). したがって draws a logical conclusion and belongs in argument, so it makes a story sound like a proof.

lessons.title: そうにない / っこない / ようがない

cases.situation: Dismissing something out of hand, among friends.
cases.guidance: Use っこない. It is blunt spoken denial ('no way that's happening'). そうにない is a neutral assessment that something looks unlikely, so it lacks the dismissiveness and is the one to use in writing.

cases.situation: There is genuinely no means of doing it.
cases.guidance: Use ようがない: 連絡しようがない. It says no method exists, which is a statement about the world. ものか is a rhetorical refusal ('as if I would'), which is a statement about your own will.

lessons.title: さえ〜ば / ものなら

cases.situation: Wishing for something you do not expect to be possible.
cases.guidance: Use ものなら: 戻れるものなら戻りたい. It marks the condition as barely attainable, which is where the wistfulness comes from. さえ〜ば says one condition would be sufficient, and treats it as perfectly achievable.

lessons.title: に限ったことではない / に限ったことでもない

cases.situation: Choosing between the ではない and でもない endings.
cases.guidance: Very little separates these. ではない is the plain denial and the one to default to; でもない softens it slightly, conceding the point rather than correcting it. Either is accepted wherever the other is.

lessons.title: ずくめ / に限る

cases.situation: Recommending something as the best there is.
cases.guidance: Use に限る: 夏はビールに限る. It is a recommendation, not a description. ずくめ describes a state made up entirely of one thing (いいことずくめ), so it reports rather than advises.

lessons.title: ようかまいか / ようがまいが

cases.situation: It makes no difference which way it goes.
cases.guidance: Use ようが〜まいが. The が pairing says the outcome holds either way. The か pairing (ようか〜まいか) is indecision: you are still weighing the two, and no outcome has been asserted yet.

lessons.title: とされる / とみられる

cases.situation: Reporting a current assessment that could still be revised.
cases.guidance: とみられる reports how something is currently viewed, often on provisional evidence, which is why news writing uses it for ongoing stories. とされる states an established or official position, so it claims more settled ground.

lessons.title: なくして〜はない / なしでは〜ない

cases.situation: A practical dependency rather than a conceptual one.
cases.guidance: Use なしでは for things you actually need to hand (眼鏡なしでは読めない). なくして is abstract and rhetorical (努力なくして成功はない), so applying it to glasses sounds like a slogan.
